analysis.title: The benign inflation scenario
key_insights: A recent US survey found almost 15% of consumers expect (or claim to expect) inflation above 15% in the coming year. US inflation has not been above 15% for over 79 years.
Consumers' focus on high-frequency purchases creates a perverse inflation perception that diverges from structural inflation.

For economists, structural problems that cause inflation to linger matter most. Observing them requires removing one-off shocks such as oil prices, which is not easy because oil affects prices broadly.
Soaring airfares and higher goods prices from diesel's effect on shipping costs result from the Gulf war. They are unlikely to continue long term unless the oil price keeps rising.
Median inflation (the midpoint of the weighted range of prices) is used as a measure of structural inflation risk. UBS calls it imperfect but reasonable.

US median inflation has been falling to near pre-pandemic norms. The decline reflects the end of the temporary boost from tariffs, which, like higher oil, have a modest effect on many prices and so raised the median.
European and UK median inflation rates have been largely stable during the Gulf war.
UBS concludes that the spin of inflation perceptions is troubling but structural inflation is less worrying.

macro_indicators.reading: Falling to near pre-pandemic norms (no figure given)
macro_indicators.interpretation: The temporary tariff boost to median inflation has ended, which points to limited structural inflation pressure in the US.

macro_indicators.reading: Largely stable during the Gulf war (no figure given)
macro_indicators.interpretation: The Gulf war oil shock has not moved structural inflation in Europe or the UK.

macro_indicators.reading: Almost 15% of consumers expect inflation over 15% in the coming year
macro_indicators.interpretation: Perceived inflation is far above the structural measures. The report attributes this to consumers' focus on high-frequency purchases.

risk_factors: A continued rise in the oil price would make the Gulf war's inflation effects, such as airfares and shipping costs, persist longer term.
geopolitical: Gulf war: oil prices, airfares and diesel-driven shipping costs have risen as a result, with effects described as unlikely to persist unless oil keeps rising.

key_data_points.metric: Share of US consumers expecting inflation over 15% in the coming year
key_data_points.context: Result of a recent US survey. UBS notes it may reflect consumers claiming they expect it.
key_data_points.anchor: almost 15% of consumers expect (or claim they expect) inflation of over 15% in the coming year

key_data_points.metric: Time since US inflation was last over 15%
key_data_points.context: Contrasts with the survey's inflation expectations.
key_data_points.anchor: It has been over 79 years since inflation was last over 15%.

tension_points.bull_case: Structural inflation is benign. US median inflation is falling to near pre-pandemic norms and European and UK medians are stable during the Gulf war.
tension_points.bear_case: Consumers' inflation perceptions are far above reality. Oil-driven costs such as airfares and shipping could linger if the oil price keeps rising.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A continued rise in the oil price, which would make the Gulf war-related price increases persist.

theme_stances.key_argument: US median inflation has fallen to near pre-pandemic norms as the temporary tariff boost ended, and European and UK medians are stable.
theme_stances.evidence: US median inflation has been falling to near pre-pandemic norms.
